p: Insects are everywhere. Scientists have named about 1 million kinds, and they think millions more are still waiting to be found.

For every one person on Earth, there are more than a billion insects. Scientists think that if you put all the insects in the world on one giant scale, they would weigh more than all the people. Small animals, but a mighty crowd.
pages.cap: One bee out of trillions and trillions of insects on Earth.
pages.fact: Did you know? About 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth. That is a 2 with 16 zeros after it.

pages.h: Six legs and a suit of armour
p: How do you know a bug is an insect? Count the legs. Every insect has six.

An insect's body has three parts: a head, a middle and a back end. Its skeleton is on the outside, like a hard suit of armour. When it grows, it must split the old suit and crawl out in a new, bigger one. Most insects have two feelers called antennae.
pages.cap: An insect's left side matches its right side, like a mirror.
pages.fact: Did you know? Insects taste with their feet. A fly tastes your sandwich just by landing on it.

p: A spider has eight legs and two body parts. So a spider is not an insect. Neither is a centipede or a worm.

Scientists put insects, spiders, crabs and centipedes in one big group called arthropods. That means jointed legs. Insects are the biggest part of the group by far. Of all the kinds of animals on Earth, more than half are insects.
pages.cap: Insects have six legs. Spiders have eight. Crabs have ten.
pages.fact: Did you know? Butterflies and beetles are insects. Ticks and scorpions are not.

pages.q: How many legs does an insect have?
pages.why: All insects have six legs. Spiders have eight, so they are not insects.

p: A butterfly starts as a tiny egg on a leaf. Out comes a caterpillar, which eats and eats. A monarch caterpillar grows 2,000 times heavier in two weeks.
Then it hangs upside down and turns into a chrysalis. Inside, its body melts and rebuilds. About ten days later, the case splits open. A butterfly with wet wings crawls out, dries off, and flies.
pages.cap: Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. Four lives in one.
pages.fact: Did you know? A monarch chrysalis has a row of tiny gold dots. Scientists are still not sure what they are for.

p: A flea is smaller than a sesame seed, yet it can leap more than 100 times its own length. If you could do that, you would jump right over a 30-storey building.
A honeybee visits flowers to drink sweet nectar. Back at the hive, bees pass the nectar from mouth to mouth and fan it with their wings until it thickens into honey.
One bee makes only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life. A jar of honey is the work of thousands of bees. Bees beat their wings about 200 times every second.
pages.cap: A bee carries nectar and pollen home from a flower.
pages.fact: Did you know? A bee tells other bees where the flowers are by doing a waggle dance.

p: When a bee lands on a flower, yellow pollen dust sticks to its fuzzy body. At the next flower, some pollen rubs off. That is how the plant makes seeds and fruit.
Apples, blueberries, pumpkins and almonds all need insects to do this. About one in every three bites of food you eat depends on a pollinator. No bugs, no blueberries.
pages.cap: A flower, a visit from a bee, and then fruit and seeds.
pages.fact: Did you know? Chocolate comes from cacao flowers that are pollinated by tiny flies the size of a pinhead.

p: Be a scientist for ten minutes.
steps: Find a patch of flowers on a sunny, warm day.
Sit still about one metre away. Set a timer for ten minutes.
Every time an insect lands on a flower, make a tally mark. Try to note what kind: bee, fly, butterfly, beetle, other.
Count your marks. Which kind came most?
Try again in the morning and in the afternoon. Is it different?
pages.cap: Sit still, watch, and count. That is real science.
pages.safe: Watch bees, do not touch them. If you are allergic to stings, watch from farther away.

pages.q: What does a bee carry from flower to flower that helps plants make fruit?
pages.why: Pollen sticks to the bee and rubs off on the next flower. That lets the plant make seeds and fruit.

p: An ant can lift about 50 times its own weight. If you were that strong, you could carry a small car over your head.

Ants live in big families called colonies. One queen lays all the eggs. The workers, all female, find food, dig tunnels and care for the babies. They talk by smell, leaving scent trails for others to follow. That is why ants march in a line.
pages.cap: Like a lever, an ant's strong jaws and legs lift loads far bigger than itself.
pages.fact: Did you know? One ant colony in Europe stretches 6,000 kilometres along the coast. Its ants all treat each other as family.

p: Some ants are farmers. Leafcutter ants in South America snip leaves and carry them home. They do not eat the leaves. They chew them into a mush and grow a fungus on it. Then they eat the fungus.
Other ants keep tiny insects called aphids like cows, and milk them for sweet juice. Ant nests can have hundreds of rooms and go 8 metres deep.
pages.cap: An ant nest is like a castle underground, with rooms for eggs, food and the queen.
pages.fact: Did you know? Army ants make bridges and nests out of their own bodies, holding on to each other with their legs.

p: You breathe with your nose and lungs. Insects have no lungs at all.

Along the sides of an insect's body are tiny holes. Air goes in through the holes and runs down tubes to every part of its body. This works well for small bodies, but it does not work for big ones. That is one reason there are no insects as big as a dog.
pages.cap: You breathe with lungs. An insect breathes through tiny holes in its sides.
pages.fact: Did you know? Insects have no red blood. Their blood is clear or yellow-green, and it does not carry air.

pages.h: Wings as wide as your arms
p: Long before dinosaurs, about 300 million years ago, a dragonfly flew with wings 70 centimetres across. The air had more oxygen then, so insects could grow huge.

pages.q: What do leafcutter ants do with the leaves they cut?
opts: Grow a fungus on them to eat
pages.why: Leafcutter ants are farmers. They chew the leaves into mush and grow fungus on it for food.

p: On summer nights, fireflies blink in the dark. A firefly is a beetle with a light in its tail.

The light comes from a chemical mix inside its body. It is cold light. Almost all the energy becomes light, and almost none becomes heat. An old light bulb does the opposite. Most of its energy is wasted as heat. Each kind of firefly has its own blinking pattern, like a secret code.
pages.cap: A light bulb gets hot. A firefly's light stays cool.
pages.fact: Did you know? In some places in Asia, thousands of fireflies on one tree all blink at the same moment.

p: At night, bats hunt moths. A bat sends out clicks and listens for the echo bouncing back. That tells it where the moth is.

But some moths can hear the bat's clicks. When a click gets close, the moth folds its wings and drops like a stone. Some tiger moths even click back, to jam the bat's hearing. It is a battle that has been going on for millions of years.
pages.cap: A bat's clicks bounce off things. Some moths can hear them coming.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some moths have fuzzy wings that soak up sound, like a quiet carpet, so bats cannot find them.

p: What happens to insects when snow falls? Some hide under bark or leaves and go to sleep. Some have a kind of antifreeze in their blood, so they do not freeze solid.
Monarch butterflies leave. Each autumn, monarchs from Canada fly more than 4,000 kilometres to the mountains of Mexico. They hang in the trees by the millions until spring.
pages.cap: In autumn, the leaves fall and the monarchs fly south.
pages.fact: Did you know? The monarchs that fly to Mexico have never been there. Their great-grandparents made the trip the year before.

pages.h: Try it: build a bug hotel
p: Give insects a safe place to rest.
steps: Find an old pot or a small wooden box with no lid.
Pack it with hollow stems, pine cones, small sticks and rolled-up cardboard.
Put it on its side in a quiet corner of a garden or balcony, out of the rain.
Check it every week. Who has moved in?
Leave a patch of dead leaves nearby. Many bugs sleep under them.
pages.cap: Hollow stems make cosy rooms for wild bees and ladybirds.
pages.safe: Ask an adult to help cut sticks, and wash your hands after.

p: What happens to a dead leaf, a fallen apple or an animal's poo? Insects eat it. Beetles, flies and ants break it down into soil.

A dung beetle rolls a ball of poo bigger than itself, then buries it to feed its babies. One kind of dung beetle can pull more than 1,000 times its own weight. Without these bugs, the ground would be buried in waste.
pages.cap: Plants feed animals. Animals feed insects. Insects turn it all back into soil.
pages.fact: Did you know? Australia had to bring in dung beetles from other countries to clean up after its cows.

pages.q: How does a moth escape a hunting bat?
opts: It hears the bat's clicks and dives
pages.why: Many moths can hear bat clicks. When a bat gets close, they fold their wings and drop out of the way.

p: Look closely at a fly's eye. It is made of thousands of tiny eyes packed together. A dragonfly has about 30,000 in each eye.

Insect eyes see fast. A fly sees your hand coming in slow motion, which is why it is so hard to swat. Bees also see colours you cannot. Many flowers have hidden patterns that only a bee can see, like a landing strip pointing to the nectar.
pages.cap: Bees see the rainbow differently. They cannot see red, but they can see a colour beyond violet.
pages.fact: Did you know? A fly can see about four times faster than you can.

p: Scientists in Germany counted flying insects in the same places for 27 years. By the end, three out of every four had vanished.

Why? Fields with no wild flowers, sprays that kill bugs, bright lights at night, and a warming world. This matters, because birds, frogs and fish eat insects. Fewer bugs means fewer birds. The good news is that bugs come back fast when we give them a chance.
pages.cap: Kids all over the world are planting flowers and counting bugs to help.
pages.fact: Did you know? When people stop mowing a lawn for one month in spring, many more bees come to visit.

p: You do not need a big garden to help insects. Plant flowers in a pot. Bees love lavender, sunflowers and clover.

Leave fallen leaves in a corner in autumn. Many bugs sleep under them. Turn off outside lights at night. Skip bug sprays. Put out a shallow dish of water with pebbles in it, so bees can drink without falling in. Small helpers for small animals.
pages.cap: A pot of flowers on a balcony is a restaurant for bees.
pages.fact: Did you know? One sunflower head is really hundreds of tiny flowers, so it feeds many bees at once.

p: Insects make things people love. Silk comes from a caterpillar. The silkworm spins a cocoon from one single thread up to 900 metres long. People unwind it to make silk cloth.
Honey and beeswax come from bees. Some red food colouring comes from a tiny bug called cochineal. And ladybirds guard gardens. One ladybird can eat 5,000 aphids in its life.
pages.cap: A silkworm moth starts as a caterpillar that spins silk.
pages.fact: Did you know? It takes about 2,500 cocoons to make one silk dress.
